name: Umbrian
confidence_why: Modern Italic specialists agree that Umbrian kept the old Italic stress on the first syllable into the historical period (Wallace 2008, following Meiser 1986; Nishimura 2014), but the whole question is an inference from spelling and syncope in an extinct language, Nishimura 2014 gives his conclusion for Umbrian "with some reservations", and the standard nineteenth-century grammar (von Planta 1892) concluded instead for a Latin-type stress on a heavy penult or otherwise the antepenult.

catalog_quote: [Wallace 2008 sec. 3.5, p.106:] Very little is known about the word accent of any Sabellian language. Nevertheless, it is possible to make informed inferences about accentuation based on orthographic practices and on certain phonological processes that affected the Sabellian languages, in particular Oscan and Umbrian, at various stages in their development. In all Sabellian languages short vowels were lost before word-final ∗s . Short vowels in open medial syllables were also syncopated before the historic period. This vocalic instability suggests that Sabellian had a stress accent which was positioned on the initial syllable of words. new_statements.translation: [p. 592] it can hardly be doubted that in Oscan-Umbrian too the so-called older Latin accentuation, which stressed the first syllable of the word, once prevailed. [...] a younger mode of accentuation, the three-syllable law (the accent cannot go back beyond the antepenult) and the rule of the penult (if the penult is short the stress rests on the antepenult, if long, on the penult itself) [...] [p. 596] they nevertheless seem sufficient to make it decidedly probable that in Oscan-Umbrian in the historical period the younger Latin accentuation prevailed.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Umbrian as fixed: initial syllable (initial stress, anchored on Wallace 2008:106 and Nishimura 2014:186, both resting on Meiser 1986:150, that the initial/radical accent was 'still in place during the historical period'). Von Planta agrees that the prehistoric Oscan-Umbrian accent was initial, but for the historical period he concludes for the Latin-type weight-sensitive penult/antepenult system, i.e. a different placement and a different type (weight-sensitive rather than fixed). The catalog's own check note already lists von Planta 1892 as 'read: contradicts the catalog's classification' and says the older analysis is carried in the record's secondary rule; this compilat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two stages. Prehistorically (Proto-Italic) the accent was on the first syllable of the word, as in Old Latin, shown by syncope in antepenults and heavy penults (Umbr. mersto- < *medesto-, Puprike- < *Puperike-) and by the contraction in mestru < *maistra. For the historical period (the Iguvine Tables) von Planta judges it 'decidedly probable' that the Latin penultimate law held: stress on the penult if it is long (by nature or position), otherwise on the antepenult, never further back. His Umbrian-specific evidence for the younger system is Puemune (ou > u presupposes an unstressed first syllable), uncontracted ahesnes/aesnes, and stahitu; the bulk of the evidence is Oscan (degemination in aamanaffed, medicatud, dadikatted, prufatted; zicolo-). The change to the younger accent postdates the syncope (Anagtiai, mersto-) and the weakening in prehubia and was not Proto-Italic but spread by wave across the already separated dialects (p. 596).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 595 n. 1: the kk of Oscan dekkviarim 'könnte aus einem Nebenton der ersten Silbe erklärt werden' (could be explained from a secondary stress on the first syllable), cited from Thurneysen on Latin; a possible initial secondary stress, offered only as a possibility and only for an Oscan form.
new_statements.exceptions: Von Planta weighs and rejects the counter-evidence for retained initial stress in the historical period: final-syllable syncope (Umbr. fons, Ikuvins, pihaz; Osk. Bantins) can be explained from either accent (p. 592 and n. 1); Tesonocir ~ Tesenocir has 'sehr geringe' probative force (p. 593 and n. 1); modern place names with odd accent (Terni, Teramo, Termoli < Interamna) point to an accent Interamna, not to initial stress (pp. 593-594). He grants that not all his own arguments are of equal value (p. 596) and that the date of the change can only be fixed relative to the syncope.
new_statements.identity_note: Von Planta treats 'Oskisch-Umbrisch' as one object and the section covers the whole Sabellic group (Oscan, Umbrian, Paelignian, Marrucinian, Volscian, Sabine); most of the evidence for the historical-period younger accent is Oscan (Tabula Bantina, Cippus Abellanus), and the specifically Umbrian material (Iguvine Tables: mersto-, Puprike-, mestru, prehubia, Puemune, ahesnes, stahitu, Tesonocir, fons, Ikuvins, pihaz) is a minority of the examples. The statement is therefore about Umbrian only as part of the Oscan-Umbrian group; it does not single out a dialect of Umbrian.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, already known to the catalog's check: von Planta 1892 (sec. 257, pp. 592-596), the only work opened here, holds that Oscan-Umbrian had initial stress prehistorically but that in the historical period the younger Latin accent (penult if heavy, otherwise antepenult) prevailed, 'entschieden wahrscheinlich'; the catalog's deciding sources (Wallace 2008:106; Nishimura 2014:186, both citing Meiser 1986:150) hold that the initial/radical accent was still in place in the historical period, Nishimura 'with some reservations' for Umbrian. Von Planta's case rests mainly on Oscan degemination; his Umbrian-specific items (Puemune, ahesnes, stahitu) are few and he concedes the arguments are of unequal value. Both sides agree the language is extinct and every statement is inference from syncope, contraction and orthography.
